title: Refugees and the Hijra
hook: the Prophet's own leaving of home, and the people on the roads today

segments.voice: Yesterday, ramadan under the midnight sun, and a family waiting for a sunset that wouldn't come. Estimate its measure. Today, a different kind of leaving. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

Two men in a cave, with the people hunting them somewhere outside. Outside is the city they grew up in, and it no longer wants them. One of them is afraid. The other says, in Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." The two are the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his friend Abu Bakr, and the journey they are on is the Hijra, the leaving of Mecca for Medina. It is a story of the past. Today it is also a story about the people on the roads right now.
screen: `TWO MEN IN A CAVE.` → `GRIEVE NOT.` → `THE HIJRA: LEAVING HOME.`

segments.voice: Hijra is the Arabic word for this leaving. It was not a holiday. The Qur'an, in the chapter called Exile, speaks of the migrants as poor, driven out from their homes and their belongings. Tradition says the Muslim calendar counts its years from this leaving. Now look at who met them. The people of Medina, the Ansar, the helpers, took the newcomers into their homes. The next verse of that chapter praises them. In Pickthall's words, they "prefer (the fugitives) above themselves though poverty become their lot." Fugitives: that's Pickthall's word for the migrants. And al-Bukhari keeps a scene from those days. One of the helpers, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', was paired as a brother with one of the newcomers, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and offered him half of everything he owned. 'Abd al-Rahman thanked him and said, in paraphrase: just show me the way to the market. A welcome on one side. Dignity on the other. The Qur'an also speaks of someone outside the faith who asks for protection. Surah nine says that if one of the idolaters seeks protection, he is to be protected and then escorted somewhere safe. So when Muslims today look at families crossing borders with what they can carry, some see the Hijra again: a Prophet who was himself once a refugee, and a city that made room. The mirror works both ways. It asks what it is to flee, and what it is to be the Ansar.
screen: `HIJRA: LEAVING A PLACE.` · `THE ANSAR MADE ROOM.` · `SHOW ME THE WAY TO THE MARKET.` · `PROTECT THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · then, large: `THEY PREFER THE FUGITIVES ABOVE THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember a leaving. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you left somewhere: a home, a school, a country, a job. What did you carry? Who met you on the other side, or who didn't? Stay with that for a few breaths. Then think of someone, anywhere, who left home this year with no choice, and arrived somewhere with very little. Hold them for a while. You don't need a name. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayers. Then choose one small thing you could give, time or money or a coat, to a group that helps refugees. The bell holds the time.
Refugees and the Hijra. The Prophet's forced leaving of Mecca, the welcome in Medina, and the mirror it holds up to people fleeing home today. Today's word.

Your line: the hijra today. Today, give something, however small, to a group that helps refugees, or learn the name of one near you. Tomorrow, poverty and zakat today. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some Muslim charities and mosques support refugees, and some teachers point to the Hijra and to the Ansar of Medina, who took the migrants into their homes, when they speak about welcoming people who have fled.

fork.setup: you've just arrived in Medina with almost nothing. your new brother from the Ansar offers you half of everything he owns. what do you say?
options: thank him, and ask the way to the market.
refuse to speak to him out of pride.
fork.reveal: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf thanked Sa'd and asked to be shown the market. a generous welcome, and a newcomer who wanted to stand on his own feet.

original.note: Arabic: a leaving or migration; above all, the Prophet's move from Mecca to Medina.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Hijra is a date on the Muslim calendar.
what it means: a forced leaving of home, and a city that made room for the people who fled.
what a scholar hears: 9:40's 'Grieve not', the Ansar of 59:9 preferring the fugitives above themselves, and the brotherhood of Sa'd and 'Abd al-Rahman in al-Bukhari.

notes: The outline hook ('many of the world's refugees are Muslim') is a statistic and was left out under the claims rule; the script speaks only of 'families crossing borders'.
Confirm Pickthall's exact wording of 9:40 ('Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.') and 59:9; confirm 'Exile' as Pickthall's name for surah 59.

'The word hijra means leaving, departing' is a dictionary sense of the word, not a derivation; confirm the phrasing. 'Tradition says the Muslim calendar counts its years from this leaving' is attributed, not sourced to a text.
Confirm Bukhari 3780 (or the parallel at 2048/5072) for Sa'd and 'Abd al-Rahman.
9:6 (protecting the idolater who seeks protection) is paraphrased; 'the very people fighting the believers' reads the verse in its context of surah 9; confirm.
'A Prophet who was himself once a refugee' are framing lines; a Keeper may prefer 'migrant' to 'refugee'.

Editor: the hijra word-meaning (etymology) and the unsourced 'left because staying was dangerous, arrived with little' are replaced by a paraphrase of 59:8 (poor, driven from homes and belongings), now cited; 'that's how the verse names the migrants' corrected, since '(the fugitives)' is Pickthall's bracketed supplement; 9:6 no longer adds 'the very people fighting the believers'; a myth item calling the Hijra unplanned (the hadith describe planning) was replaced; the cave hook no longer claims pursuers 'close enough to hear'.
